title: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
summary: How to verify agent output before shipping it: layered checks from schemas to tests to LLM judges, best-of-N math with an imperfect verifier, why more samples can hurt, and why self-correction needs external feedback.
outcomes: Explain why an agent's report of success is not evidence and how test-based ground truth like SWE-bench decides resolved
Order deterministic, executable and judged checks into a cascade and compute its expected cost per candidate
Compute best-of-N accuracy from a verifier's TPR and FPR and show it converges to the verifier's precision
Explain why argmax selection against an exploitable verifier can get worse with more samples, and how CodeT uses agreement
Explain why intrinsic self-correction often lowers accuracy and design a loop grounded in external feedback

lessons.title: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done

blocks.md: In the agent harness course an agent was an LLM in a loop: it reads context, emits a structured tool call, the harness runs the tool and appends the result, and the loop repeats until the model says it is finished. That final "I fixed the bug, all tests pass" is just more generated text. Nothing in the loop has checked it.

Long action chains make this worse. Anthropic's guide *Building effective agents* warns that the autonomy of agents means higher costs and the potential for **compounding errors**, and recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments with guardrails. A toy model shows why: if each of 20 steps is right with probability 0.95 and errors are independent, the whole run is right with probability $0.95^{20} \approx 0.358$. Real errors are not independent, but the direction is the same: long runs fail more often than single steps suggest.

A **verifier** is any procedure that takes the task and a candidate result (sometimes the whole trajectory) and returns pass or fail, or a score. Verifiers are used in four ways:

- **Gate**: decide whether to ship, merge or execute a result.
- **Select**: generate several candidates and keep the one the verifier prefers.
- **Feedback**: send the verifier's findings back to the agent for another attempt.
- **Reward**: score trajectories to train the model (covered in RL courses, not here).

blocks.title: Where a verifier sits around an agent

scenes.caption: Without verification the agent's own claim of success is the only signal. The harness would ship whatever the loop produced.
A verifier sits between the candidate and any irreversible action. It looks at evidence (test results, schemas, outputs), not at the agent's description of its work.
Pass: the result is shipped. The verifier's false positive rate now decides how many wrong results slip through this gate.
Fail: the specific findings go back into the agent's context for another attempt. When the verifier cannot decide, a human is the last layer.

blocks.md: The cleanest example of ground truth for agents is SWE-bench (Jimenez et al.). Each of its 2,294 tasks is a real GitHub issue in one of 12 Python repositories. The model edits the codebase; the benchmark applies the patch with `patch` and runs the repository's tests. The task counts as resolved only if the patch applies and all of those tests pass.

Two kinds of tests make that judgment. **Fail-to-pass** tests fail before the reference fix and pass after it, so they check that the issue is addressed; every task has at least one and 40% have at least two. **Pass-to-pass** tests (a median of 51 per task) passed before and must still pass, so they check that nothing else broke.

blocks.title: How SWE-bench style evaluation decides resolved

scenes.caption: The agent hands over a patch. Its own claims about tests are ignored; only the harness's run counts.
The harness applies the patch to a clean copy of the repository at the task's base commit. A patch that does not apply is already a failure.
Fail-to-pass tests run first in this picture: they must now pass, showing the issue is fixed.
Pass-to-pass tests guard old behavior. One regression here and the task is not resolved, even though the issue itself was fixed.

blocks.md: Verification turns "the agent says it is done" into "independent evidence says it is done". How much you can trust a shipped result is bounded by how often the verifier passes wrong results.

Misconception: if the agent ran the tests itself and reported success, the work is verified. The report is model output, and tests the agent wrote or could edit are not independent. Run the checks in the harness, on a clean copy, with tests the agent did not control.

blocks.question: An agent's final message says: "Fixed the parser; I ran pytest and everything passes." The harness has not run anything. What do you actually know?
options: The fix is verified, since the agent observed a passing pytest run
Nothing is verified yet: the message is generated text until the harness runs the tests itself
The fix is verified if the agent's message includes the pytest output
The fix is half verified: the tests pass but the code was not reviewed
blocks.explain: Everything in the final message, including pasted output, is produced by the model and may be wrong or stale. Evidence comes from the harness running checks it controls on the actual workspace.

blocks.question: A SWE-bench patch makes all fail-to-pass tests pass but breaks one pass-to-pass test. How is it scored?
options: Resolved, because the issue's own tests pass
Partially resolved, scored by the fraction of tests passing
Not resolved, because all of the task's tests must pass
Resolved if the broken test is in a different file
blocks.explain: SWE-bench counts a task as resolved only if the patch applies and all associated tests pass. Pass-to-pass tests exist precisely to catch fixes that break existing behavior.

lessons.title: Layer the checks: deterministic first, judges last

blocks.md:
Verifiers come in three families, ordered by how much you can trust them and how much they cost:

1. **Structural checks**: parse the output, validate it against a schema, type check, lint, or assert invariants such as "the diff only touches files under src/". Deterministic, nearly free, and they never disagree with themselves.
2. **Executable checks**: run unit tests, run the program on inputs, or diff the environment state against the expected state. They test behavior, but only on the cases the tests cover.
3. **Judged checks**: an LLM judge with a rubric, or a human reviewer. They cover fuzzy criteria (is this summary faithful, is the tone right) but are noisy, biased and the most expensive per call.

Each family answers a narrower question than it seems. Valid JSON can still contain the wrong flight; passing tests can still miss an untested branch; an approving judge can be swayed by length. That is why they are stacked, and why the order matters.

blocks.caption: A three-layer cascade with early exit. jsonschema.validate raises ValidationError on a mismatch; pytest returns exit code 0 only when all collected tests pass.

blocks.title: A cascade filters before the expensive layer

scenes.caption: Simplified cost model in arbitrary units: schema check 0.01, test run 1, LLM judge 5 per candidate. 100 candidates arrive.
The schema check runs on all 100 and rejects 20 malformed outputs for a total cost of 1. The rejection reason is exact and can be fed back.
Only the 80 survivors pay for a test run (cost 80). Half fail. Executable evidence removes most wrong candidates before any judge sees them.
The judge runs on 40 candidates (cost 200) instead of 100 (cost 500). Total 281, which is 2.81 per candidate versus 6.01 with no early exit.

blocks.caption: Expected cost per candidate of a cascade with early exit, where P_1 and P_2 are the pass rates of the first two layers. Running every layer on every candidate costs 0.01 + 1 + 5 = 6.01.

blocks.title: Cost per candidate by layer (simplified units)

scenes.caption: No early exit: every candidate pays for every layer, 6.01 in total. The judge dominates.
Cheap first with early exit: the judge's share falls from 5 to 2.0 because only 40% of candidates reach it. Total 2.81.

blocks.md: Stacking also changes error rates. Treat each layer as a test with a **true positive rate** (TPR: fraction of correct results it passes) and a **false positive rate** (FPR: fraction of wrong results it passes). A result is accepted only if every layer passes it, so if layer errors were independent the rates multiply. With TPRs 0.99, 0.95, 0.9 and FPRs 0.5, 0.1, 0.3, the chain has TPR $0.846$ and FPR $0.015$. Each layer cuts false positives, but each also rejects some good results.

The multiplication assumes independent errors, which is optimistic. A judge and a test suite written from the same misunderstanding of the spec fail on the same wrong answers, so the real chain FPR is higher than the product.

The judge goes last because its errors are the least predictable. Zheng et al. (MT-Bench) measured: when two similar answers were swapped in order, GPT-4 as judge gave a consistent verdict in only 65% of cases; a "repetitive list" attack that pads an answer with a reworded copy of its own list fooled Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 in 91.3% of cases and GPT-4 in 8.7%; and on 10 math questions GPT-4 approved wrong answers in 14 of 20 trials with the default prompt, 6 with chain of thought, and 3 when given a reference solution.

Make judges cheaper to trust: give the judge a reference answer or the test log when one exists, ask about one criterion per call, and for pairwise judgments run both orders and count a win only when both agree (the mitigation Zheng et al. propose).

blocks.question: An agent fills a booking form and must output JSON with a date, a flight number in a fixed format, and a price within the user's budget. Which verification plan fits best?
options: Ask a strong LLM judge whether the booking looks right, since it can check all three fields at once
Validate the JSON schema and regex, check the price and date with code, then use a judge only for whether the flight matches the user's stated preferences
Re-ask the same agent to double-check its JSON before submitting
Skip checks for the format and only verify the price, since format errors are rare
blocks.explain: Format, ranges and arithmetic are deterministic: code checks them exactly and almost for free. A judge is reserved for the fuzzy part (preferences) that code cannot express.

blocks.question: In the cascade above, the team moves the LLM judge to the first position (it still rejects some candidates). What happens to the expected cost per candidate?
options: It stays 2.81, since the same checks run
It drops, because the judge filters bad candidates early
It becomes at least 5, because every candidate now pays for the judge
It becomes exactly 6.01 regardless of pass rates
blocks.explain: With early exit the first layer always runs on every candidate. Putting the 5-unit judge first means each candidate pays at least 5 before the cheap checks get a chance to reject it, versus 2.81 with cheap checks first.

lessons.title: Best-of-N with an imperfect verifier: the accuracy ceiling

blocks.md: **Generate then verify** means sampling $N$ candidates for the same task and letting a verifier pick one. Cobbe et al. introduced the GSM8K grade-school math dataset (8.5K problems) and trained verifiers to judge whether a sampled solution was correct. At test time they sampled 100 solutions per problem and returned the one ranked highest. A 6B model with a verifier slightly outperformed a fine-tuned 175B model, about the same boost as a 30x larger model.

How much can selection help? Start with a binary verifier and a simple probability model. Each candidate is correct with probability $p$, independently. The verifier passes a correct candidate with probability $t$ (its TPR, also called recall) and passes a wrong one with probability $f$ (its FPR). The selector picks uniformly among candidates that pass; if none pass it picks any candidate at random.

blocks.title: Eight candidates through an imperfect verifier

scenes.caption: The agent produces 8 candidates for one task. Their correctness is hidden from the selector; it only sees verifier verdicts.
Ground truth, which only an oracle knows: candidates 0 and 3 are correct, the other six are wrong. Coverage (some candidate is correct) is already achieved.
The verifier passes both correct candidates (true positives) and also candidate 5, a wrong one (a false positive). The other wrong ones are rejected.
The selector picks among the 3 passers, so it returns a correct answer with probability 2/3 here. More samples add more passers, but the mix of right and wrong passers stays the same on average.

blocks.prompt: Let $p = 0.3$, TPR $t = 0.9$, FPR $f = 0.1$. As $N$ grows without limit, at least one candidate is almost surely correct. Does best-of-N accuracy approach 1?
blocks.reveal: No. It approaches **0.794**. Once many candidates pass, the pick is a random passer, and a random passer is correct with probability $pt / (pt + (1-p)f) = 0.27 / 0.34$. That ratio is the verifier's **precision** on this candidate distribution, and no amount of sampling raises it.

blocks.caption: c is the probability a single candidate fails the verifier. With probability 1 - c^N at least one passes and the pick is a random passer; otherwise the pick is a random failed candidate. At N = 1 this equals p.

blocks.md: Worked example with $p = 0.3$, $t = 0.9$, $f = 0.1$: a candidate is a correct passer with probability $0.27$, a wrong passer with probability $0.07$, and fails with $c = 0.66$. Accuracy is 0.300 at $N = 1$, 0.652 at $N = 4$, 0.767 at $N = 8$, 0.793 at $N = 16$, and the limit is 0.794. A perfect verifier would instead reach the **coverage** $1 - (1-p)^N$: 0.760 at $N = 4$ and 0.942 at $N = 8$.

blocks.title: Best-of-N accuracy vs N for a verifier with given TPR and FPR

scenes.caption: TPR 0.9, FPR 0.1, p = 0.3: the curve rises quickly and flattens at the precision 0.794, while a perfect verifier keeps climbing toward 1.
A test-suite-like verifier, TPR 0.95 and FPR 0.02: the ceiling rises to 0.953 and accuracy reaches 0.950 by N = 16.
A lenient judge, TPR 0.9 but FPR 0.3: the ceiling drops to 0.563 and is reached by N = 16. Extra samples buy nothing after that.
A strict verifier, TPR only 0.5 but FPR 0.02: slower at small N (0.556 at N = 4) yet a high ceiling of 0.915 (0.873 at N = 16). Low recall costs samples; a high FPR costs accuracy.

blocks.md: FPR sets the ceiling, TPR sets the speed. With enough samples, best-of-N accuracy converges to the verifier's precision $pt / (pt + (1-p)f)$. Raising TPR only means you need fewer samples to get there.

Agents can also **abstain**: if nothing passes, escalate instead of shipping a random candidate. Then every shipped answer is a passer, so shipped accuracy equals the precision at any $N$, and $N$ controls how often you can answer at all: $1 - c^N$, which is 0.34 at $N = 1$, 0.81 at $N = 4$ and 0.96 at $N = 8$ in the worked example.

Precision also depends on $p$. The same verifier looks better on easy tasks, where most passers are correct, and worse on hard ones. Measure TPR and FPR on candidates from your own agent on your own task mix, not on someone else's benchmark.

blocks.question: With p = 0.3 and a verifier at TPR 0.9, FPR 0.1, you can afford one improvement. Which one raises the accuracy you reach at large N?
options: Raise TPR to 0.99 and keep FPR at 0.1
Lower FPR to 0.05 and keep TPR at 0.9
Double N from 32 to 64
Both of the first two raise it by the same amount
blocks.explain: The large-N limit is precision. TPR 0.99 gives 0.297/(0.297+0.07) = 0.809; FPR 0.05 gives 0.27/(0.27+0.035) = 0.885. Doubling N past 32 changes almost nothing because the curve has already reached 0.794.

blocks.question: Candidates are correct half the time (p = 0.5). A verifier has TPR 0.8 and FPR 0.2. What fraction of shipped answers are correct if the agent abstains whenever nothing passes?
blocks.explain: Shipped answers are all passers, so accuracy is precision: 0.5(0.8) / (0.5(0.8) + 0.5(0.2)) = 0.4 / 0.5 = 0.8.

lessons.title: When more samples hurt, and how agreement helps

blocks.md: The binary model plateaus but never goes down. Real verifiers often output a **score**, and the selector takes the argmax. Cobbe et al. saw something worse than a plateau: with a 6B verifier on GSM8K, accuracy improved as they increased completions up to 400, then decreased. Their explanation: the benefit of search is eventually outweighed by the risk of finding adversarial solutions that fool the verifier. They used 100 completions in most experiments.

A simplified model shows the shape. Suppose a small fraction $r$ of wrong candidates are **foolers**: they score above every correct candidate. Plain wrong candidates score below correct ones. The argmax is correct only if no fooler was sampled and at least one correct candidate was. With $s = (1-p)r$, the chance a single sample is a fooler:

blocks.caption: The first term is P(no fooler among N); subtracting the second removes the cases with no fooler and no correct candidate either. Simplified: real scores overlap more gradually.

blocks.title: Argmax selection with a verifier that rare outputs fool

scenes.caption: With p = 0.3 and one wrong answer in 1,000 able to fool the verifier, accuracy peaks at 0.986 near N = 17.
Past the peak, each extra sample is a new chance to draw a fooler. At N = 400 accuracy has fallen to 0.756 and at N = 1000 to 0.497.
With r = 0.01 the peak comes earlier (N = 11, 0.908) and the fall is steep. A more exploitable verifier needs a smaller N.
With r = 0 the verifier cannot be fooled and argmax matches the perfect-verifier curve. The decline comes entirely from exploitable verifier errors.

blocks.md: Misconception: more samples are always at least as good. Searching harder against a learned or LLM verifier is optimization against an imperfect proxy, which is reward hacking at inference time. Cap $N$ where measured accuracy peaks, not where your budget ends.

When an exact checker exists, the picture flips. Brown et al. (Large Language Monkeys) found that **coverage**, the fraction of problems solved by any sample, often grows log-linearly with the number of samples. On SWE-bench Lite, coverage for DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct rose from 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250. In domains without automatic verifiers, they found majority voting and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples.

Cobbe et al. also softened the argmax: take a majority vote over the final answers of the top-ranked solutions. With 100 samples it was best to let the top 3 to 5 vote; with 3,200 samples, about the top 30. Agreement between independent candidates is evidence a single fooler cannot fake.

CodeT (Chen et al.) applies the same idea to code without human tests. The model generates both solutions and test cases. Solutions that pass exactly the same set of generated tests form a group, and each group gets the **dual execution agreement** score $f(S) = |S_x||S_y|$: number of solutions times number of tests they pass. The best group wins. With code-davinci-002 this raised HumanEval pass@1 to 65.8%, an absolute gain of 18.8 points.

blocks.title: CodeT toy: which solutions pass which generated tests

scenes.caption: Five sampled solutions run against four model-written tests (1 = pass). Test 4 is itself wrong, which generated tests often are.
Counting tests passed alone gives a tie: solutions 1 to 4 each pass 3 tests. The count cannot tell which 3 tests are trustworthy.
Solutions 1, 2 and 3 pass the identical set {1, 2, 3}, so they behave the same. Score f(S) = 3 solutions x 3 tests = 9.
Solution 4 stands alone with tests {1, 3, 4}: score 1 x 3 = 3. Solution 5 passes nothing: score 0. CodeT returns a solution from the score-9 group.

blocks.question: A team picks the highest-scoring of N agent attempts using an LLM judge's 1 to 10 score. Moving from N = 16 to N = 256 lowers measured accuracy. What is the most likely cause?
options: Sampling noise; with more samples accuracy must eventually rise
More samples include more rare wrong answers that the judge scores highly, and argmax picks them
The judge gets tired over longer batches
The candidates got worse because temperature rose with N
blocks.explain: Argmax over a fallible score rewards outliers. The more you sample, the more likely you draw a wrong answer that exploits the judge, which is the effect Cobbe et al. saw beyond 400 completions.

blocks.question: In CodeT, group A has 2 solutions that pass the same 5 tests and group B has 6 solutions that pass the same 2 tests. Which group does dual execution agreement prefer?
options: B, because its score 6 x 2 = 12 exceeds 2 x 5 = 10
A, because its solutions pass more tests
Neither; CodeT breaks ties at random
A, because CodeT only counts tests passed
blocks.explain: The score is |Sx| times |Sy|: 12 for B and 10 for A. Agreement among many solutions counts as much as test count, which is how CodeT resists a few wrong tests.

blocks.md: A tempting shortcut is to skip external verifiers and ask the model to review its own answer. Huang et al. call this **intrinsic self-correction**: the model tries to fix its initial response using only its own capabilities, without external feedback. They prompted with variants of "Review your previous answer and find problems with your answer", for up to two rounds, then measured accuracy.

blocks.title: Accuracy before and after intrinsic self-correction (Huang et al.)

scenes.caption: Standard prompting, one call per question.
After one round of self-review (3 calls): every number drops. CommonSenseQA with GPT-3.5 falls to 38.1 as the model talks itself out of right answers.
After two rounds (5 calls): still below the start. More compute bought lower accuracy.
With oracle labels (stop as soon as the answer is correct) the same loop looks great. But that uses the ground truth, which a deployed agent does not have.

blocks.md: Earlier reports of large self-correction gains often used **oracle labels**: the loop stopped once the answer matched the ground truth. Huang et al. note that if you already have the ground truth there is little reason to run the model, so those results describe an oracle, not self-correction. Their diagnosis is blunt: the model cannot properly judge the correctness of its own reasoning. On GSM8K, GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time, and when it changed, it more often turned a correct answer wrong than a wrong answer right.
A two-number model explains why. Let $a$ be accuracy before review, $u$ the chance a review flips a correct answer to wrong, and $v$ the chance it fixes a wrong one.

blocks.caption: A review loop helps only if fixes outnumber breakages, weighted by how many answers are currently right versus wrong.

blocks.md: At $a = 0.759$ the review must be more than 3.15 times as likely to fix a wrong answer as to break a right one. At $a = 0.955$ the ratio must exceed 21.2. Even a review that fixes 10% of wrong answers and breaks only 5% of right ones lowers 0.759 to 0.745. The better the first answer, the more harmless the critic must be, which is exactly where an unaided self-critic is weakest.

blocks.prompt: Reflexion (Shinn et al.) reached 91% pass@1 on HumanEval with GPT-4 by letting the agent reflect on failures and retry. Is that intrinsic self-correction?
blocks.reveal: No. Reflexion's programming agent writes unit tests, **executes** them, and reflects on the real execution results. The interpreter is external feedback. When the authors removed test generation on the 50 hardest HumanEval Rust problems, accuracy fell to 0.52, below the 0.60 baseline, because the agent could not tell when its code was already correct and kept making harmful edits. Full Reflexion scored 0.68.

blocks.md: Reflexion also shows that external feedback is only as good as its false positive rate. Its tests are model-written. On MBPP Python, 16.3% of solutions that passed all internal tests were still wrong (one minus the verifier's precision), versus 1.4% on HumanEval Python. With that leaky verifier, Reflexion scored 77.1 on MBPP Python, below the 80.1 of GPT-4 alone, while it scored 91.0 on HumanEval. The lesson from lesson 3 again: verifier FPR caps what the loop can deliver.

Kamoi et al. surveyed the self-correction literature and concluded: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except in tasks exceptionally suited to it; (2) self-correction works well in tasks that can use reliable external feedback; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables self-correction. Huang et al. add a cost warning: compare against simple baselines with the same number of calls, since multi-agent debate did no better than self-consistency (majority vote over samples) at equal cost.

scenes.caption: Anthropic's evaluator-optimizer workflow: one LLM call generates a response while another evaluates it and gives feedback in a loop.
An evaluator with only the draft to look at is close to intrinsic self-correction: its feedback is opinion, and wrong opinions break right answers.
Ground the evaluator: run deterministic and executable checks first and hand it their logs. Now its feedback cites real failures.
Stop on a passing check or an iteration cap. The guide's fit test: clear evaluation criteria, and refinement that measurably improves results.

blocks.md: Self-correction works when the feedback carries information the generator did not have: a failing test, a compiler error, a schema violation, a human note. Asking the same model to "check again" adds calls, not information.

Putting the course together, a practical recipe for shipping agent work:

1. Run cheap structural checks on every candidate and feed exact errors back.
2. Use executable ground truth (tests the agent did not write or cannot edit, state diffs) as the main gate.
3. Use an LLM judge last, for criteria code cannot express, with a reference and order swapping.
4. Spend samples only where a verifier with low FPR exists, measure where accuracy peaks, and cap $N$ there.
5. When nothing passes, escalate instead of shipping a guess.

blocks.question: Which review loop is most likely to improve an agent's final accuracy?
options: The agent rereads its answer and is asked "Are you sure? Fix any mistakes" for three rounds
A second copy of the same model critiques the answer with no extra inputs
The agent is asked to rate its confidence and retries if below 8 of 10
The agent's code is run against a held-out test suite and the failing test output is returned for a retry
blocks.explain: Only the test run adds new, reliable information. The others ask the model to judge its own reasoning, which Huang et al. found often lowers accuracy, and Kamoi et al. found works mainly with reliable external feedback.

blocks.question: A first-pass agent is right 90% of the time. A self-review step fixes 30% of wrong answers but breaks 5% of right ones. What happens to accuracy?
options: Rises to 93%
Stays at 90%
Falls to 88.5%
Falls to 85.5%
blocks.explain: a' = 0.9(0.95) + 0.1(0.3) = 0.855 + 0.03 = 0.885. The fix rate needed to break even is v/u > 0.9/0.1 = 9, but here v/u = 6.
